item.title: Python Object IDs: Why They Reuse Memory and How to Ensure Uniqueness
item.description:
“Python Object IDs: Why They Reuse Memory and How to Ensure Uniqueness”

When working with Python, you might observe that object identifiers (obtained via the id() function) can sometimes appear to be reused. This behavior, while counterintuitive, is a direct result of Python’s memory management and object lifetime. Let’s delve into why this happens and how you can achieve guaranteed unique identifiers for your objects when necessary.

The id() function in Python returns an integer that is unique for a specific object during its lifetime. This is a crucial distinction. Two objects that do not have overlapping lifetimes can indeed share the same id() value. This often occurs when an object is created, goes out of scope, and is subsequently garbage collected. The memory previously occupied by that object can then be reallocated for a new object, leading to the new object receiving the same identifier.
